[[footnote:5]]A bazaar, with stalls of home-made goods such as pincushions and penwipers, had been held to raise funds to build a boys’ school in Otterbourne, and Anne presumably had made a bookmark with Mr Bigg-Wither’s initials on. This was a very common way of raising money for charity in Victorian England. For CMY\'s later attitude to bazaars, see the discussion by Leslee Thorne-Murphy, \'The Charity Bazaar and Women\'s Professionalization in Charlotte Mary Yonge\'s The Daisy Chain\' Studies in English Literature 1500-1900 47 (Autumn 2007) 881-9.
[[footnote:6]]Anne’s mother, Alethea Henrietta (Bargus) Yonge (1789-1844), ‘Aunt Yonge’, was half-sister of CMY’s mother. Anne herself was ‘ little a’, her elder sister Alethea (1815-1863, who married in 1845 the Rev. John Philip Anderson Morshead), ‘great A’. The allusion is to a nursery rhyme ‘Great A, little a,/ Bouncing B,/ The cat’s in the cupboard/ And she can’t see.’ Iona and Peter Opie, Oxford Dictionary of Nursery Rhymes (1951), 51.

Dyson has evidently also asked for recommendations for books suitable to be read aloud on Sundays. [[footnote:2]][[otherbook:7]Review of William Wordsworth, The Prelude] (1850) in The Christian Remembrancer XX (October 1850) 332-73, 347: \'And children left to themselves may in their innocence get no harm from what may taint an older imagination. But as a rule, it must be the duty of parents to guard their minds from contamination as much as their manners.\' [[footnote:3]]Probably Edmund Rodney Pollexfen Bastard (1825-1856) of Kitley, near Yealmpton, a neighbour of the Puslinch Yonges, mentioned in George Moberly\'s diary as having converted to Rome by January 1851 ([[otherbook:122]Dulce Domum], 94),who married a Roman Catholic in 1853. The context makes clear that Mr B is a patient of CMY’s uncle Dr. James Yonge, a Plymouth physician. [[footnote:4]]The Rev. William Maskell (1814?-1890), ecclesiastical historian, was deeply involved in the Gorham controversy over baptismal regeneration, and converted to Rome in about 1850. [[footnote:5]]The Rev. Leveson Vernon Harcourt (1788-1860), chancellor of York, and his wife, née the Hon. Caroline Peachey (d.1871), CMY\'s godmother. They lived at West Dean, in Sussex, and were neighbours of Manning, who was Rector of Lavington. [[footnote:6]]The Rev. Edward Monro, The Combatants: An Allegory (London 1848). In this story about withstanding the temptations of worldliness Eustace is the noblest but suffers most. [[footnote:7]]Harriet Martineau (1802-1876), Deerbrook (1839). Martineau had been brought up as a Unitarian. Socinians deny the divinity of Christ. [[footnote:8]]Elizabeth Gaskell (1810-1865), Mary Barton (1848), another novel by a Unitarian. [[footnote:9]]The Rev. Edward Bouverie Pusey (1800-1882), one of the founders of the Tractarian movement. Its followers were often called Puseyites. CMY met him only once, at Keble\'s funeral. He wrote a large number of letters of spiritual advice, some of which were published (but not at this date), and the Coleridges’ letters were presumably in MS. [[footnote:10]]Anne Mozley was the editor of the [[other:79]Magazine for the Young], which was aimed at a readership among working-class children. CMY had contributed her novel The Two Guardians to another organ of the Tractarian movement, [[other:62]The Churchman\'s Companion], published by Masters. The Dysons and the Yonges felt, however, that the latter was too controversial in its theology to be good for the young, and wished to start a magazine aimed at children and young people of the middle and upper classes. [[footnote:2]]Evidently a letter from Fanny’s brother, John Coleridge Patteson, who had been consecrated missionary Bishop of Melanesia by Bishop Selwyn in St. Paul’s Church, Auckland, on 24 February 1861. [[footnote:3]]William Kerr, 8th Marquess of Lothian (1832-1870), succeeded his father in 1841; his mother Cecil, Marchioness of Lothian (1808-1877) was an enthusiastic Tractarian, and financed the building of the episcopal church at Jedburgh which was consecrated in 1843, with Keble present. Her conversion to Roman Catholicism in 1851 caused a stir, but her eldest son, who is mentioned in the [[cmybook:39]Hursley Magazine] and so may have met CMY, did not follow her. The school for Melanesians founded in 1859 by Selwyn at Kohimarama (now Mission Bay), near Auckland, had been named St. Andrew’s College, in allusion to the foundation of St. Andrew’s Church in [[cmybook:24]The Daisy Chain]. The reference seems to be to Keble’s poem ‘The Boy with The Five Loaves’ in Lyra Innocentium [[footnote:4]]The sisters had taken much trouble to provide Patteson with the correct episcopal costume. He wrote to his father (1 December 1860): ‘ Dear Joan is investing moneys in cutaway coats, buckles without end, and no doubt knee-breeches and what she calls \\"gambroons ‘ (whereof I have no cognizance), none of which will be worn more than (say) four or five times in the year. Gambroons and aprons and lawn sleeves won’t go a-voyaging, depend upon it. Just when I preach in some Auckland church I shall appear in full costume; but the buckles will grow very rusty indeed!’ CMY comments in her [[cmybook:102]biography] of him that ‘in a separate letter to the sisters there are individual acknowledgments of each article of the equipment, gratifying the donor by informing her that the ‘cutaway’ coat was actually to be worn that very evening at a dinner party at the Chief Justice’s, and admiring the ‘gambroon,’ which turned out to be the material of the cassock, so much as to wish for a coat made of it for the islands.’

letter_footnote: [[footnote:1]]\'Autobiography of Prince Charles of Hesse\' Monthly Packet (May 1866) is evidently the article referred to; it is extracted from the Revue des Deux Mondes (December 1865). The addressee was no doubt the author of the piece on Mère Angélique in the second series of Biographies of Good Women, which is signed M.L.C.. Confusingly, there are two writers using these two initials during the same period. The attractive memoir Sometime in Ireland: A Recollection (London: King 1874), published as by \'M.L.C.\' and a novel This Picture and That (1886), advertised as by the author of the memoir, Mrs Charles Chapman, seem to be by Mary Lee (1814/5-1892), youngest daughter of the Very Rev. Ussher Lee, Dean of Waterford (1763/4-1850) and his wife Hannah (1774/5-1854), who married, first (1843), the Rev. John Hellier Stephenson (d.1861), Rector of Corringham, Essex, and, secondly (28 September 1866), as his second wife, the Rev. Charles Chapman (1806-1892), Rector of Acrise, Kent until 1871. However, the date of her marriage to Chapman makes it impossible she should have contributed the biography under those initials. Another candidate, also an Irishwoman, is Mary L. Code, who is listed as author of a series of children\'s books published in the early 1870s under these initials: Lonely Lily (London: Shaw 1870); Clarie’s Little Charge (London: Shaw 1871); The Happy Land, or, Willie the Orphan (London: Shaw 1872); Wandering May, or, ‘Come unto Me’ (London: Shaw 1872); and Left at Home, or, The Heart’s Resting Place (London: Shaw 1874). She appears to be Mary Louisa Code (1848/9-1873), daughter of the Rev. John Marsden Code (1805-1873), who had resigned from the Church of Ireland to become a Plymouth Brother. She was living in Bath during the 1871 census and died there a couple of years later. Unless she was much less of an evangelical than her father it seems unlikely CMY would have admitted her to the Monthly Packet, and she is rather young. It seems probable, therefore, that CMY\'s correspondent was a third woman writing under these initials.

March-Phillipps goes on to quote part of a letter from Hawker to [[person:329]Christabel Coleridge]: If Miss Yonge would only carry out her views as to what ought to be the end of the story as explained in her letter to me . . it would make an entertaining paragraph. . . .
